Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. Nobody shares their own relationship. If a student mentions being scared of a partner, or an ex threatening or sharing images, follow up privately and connect them with a counselor.

Every student in the room

Say "ex" or "someone you dated" rather than a gender, and keep in mind that some families don't allow dating, so a student may be grieving something nobody at home knew about.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can explain why a breakup can hurt this much (the wanting doesn't switch off right away), know that most people recover sooner than they predict and when a low that isn't lifting needs more help, and name one move they would use themselves or offer a friend. Nobody shares their own relationship.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 4 minMyth or true, one per slide
  2. 3 minThe relationship ended. The wanting didn’t, yet.
  3. 2 minMost people feel better sooner than they predict
  4. 5 minWhat helps: turn and talk, share out
  5. 6 minThree hard moments: Nate, Ava, Sam
  6. 5 minEvery student, where else this shows up, being the friend

Short on time (10-minute check-in)

Two myths, why it hits hard, what helps, one of the three moments, and being the friend.

Before you teach
Someone in the circle may be in it right now.

Maybe with someone else in the same advisory. Don't ask anyone to share their own relationship or breakup, and keep every couple in the grade out of the conversation. If a student starts telling their story, thank them and offer to talk after.

Not everyone has dated, and that's fine.

Frame the lesson as something everyone uses, since most students will be the friend someone texts at midnight. The closing reflection is about being that friend, so nobody needs experience to take part.

Know the signs that need a counselor.

Sadness that isn't easing after a few weeks, hopelessness, trouble eating, sleeping or getting to school. Don't ask about these in the circle. If you notice them or a student tells you, connect them with a counselor that day. 988 (call or text) is open any time, and The Trevor Project (1-866-488-7386, or text START to 678-678) is there for LGBTQ+ students.

Threats, harassment and private images go to an adult right away.

If an ex is threatening, harassing or sharing private images, that's a same-day conversation with a counselor or dean. Don't ask to see anything. In Massachusetts, sharing explicit images without consent is a crime. love is respect (text LOVEIS to 22522) helps when an ex won't leave someone alone.

Ending it in person isn't always safe.

The Sam card says "if it's safe" on purpose. If a student says a partner scares them, take it out of the room and follow up with a counselor.

Don't rank the loss.

Short relationships, secret ones and first ones can hurt a lot, and so can a breakup the student chose. Avoid "you're young, there will be others." Let it be as big as it is.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Partners can be any gender.

Say "ex," "partner" or "someone you dated," and keep the scenarios as written: none of them names a gender for the ex. A student who isn't out may be grieving a relationship nobody knew about. If home isn't safe to talk about it, a counselor can help them figure out who is.

Some families don't allow dating.

Rules about dating come from faith, culture and family, and they vary a lot. A student may have kept a relationship secret and have nobody at home to tell. Don't ask why, and don't judge their family. Name school adults as a place to bring it.

Anyone can grieve, and anyone can end it.

Nate is the one hurting and Sam is the one ending it, on purpose. Guys can cry over a breakup, girls can be the one who leaves, and nonbinary students go through all of it too. Keep "guys don't care" and "girls are dramatic" out of the room.

"Tell someone" means any adult they trust.

That could be a parent or caregiver, a grandparent, an older sibling or cousin, a coach or a counselor. Not every student lives with two parents or can bring this home, so always name a school adult too.

Rumination and routine changes hit some students harder.

Students with ADHD, anxiety or autism may find replaying thoughts, a song in the car, or a sudden change in lunch table or routine extra hard. "Keep your routine" and "script the shared spaces" help here. Pair talk can be swapped for writing for students who'd rather not speak.

Every move is free.

Muting, archiving, writing the message you won't send and keeping a routine cost nothing. When you mention distraction, say "a walk, a roll, a stretch, a show, a friend," and "the ride or walk home" so the advice fits students without a car, a gym or spending money.

What the research says

In brain scans of people recently rejected but still in love, a hub of the dopamine system lit up at a photo of their ex, much as it does in people happily in love. The researchers noted overlap with regions involved in craving; whether rejection works like addiction is still debated.

Fisher, Brown, Aron, Strong and Mashek, Journal of Neurophysiology, 2010

40 people who'd had an unwanted breakup in the past six months looked at their ex's photo in a scanner. Areas that also process physical pain became active. Other scientists argue those areas aren't pain-specific.

Kross, Berman, Mischel, Smith and Wager, PNAS, 2011

College students predicted how upset they'd be after a breakup, and those who broke up were followed. Most overestimated their distress, and the most in love overestimated it most.

Eastwick, Finkel, Krishnamurti and Loewenstein, Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 2008

In a study of 1,470 older teens, a recent romantic breakup was linked to a higher chance of a first episode of major depression.

Monroe, Rohde, Seeley and Lewinsohn, Journal of Abnormal Psychology, 1999

In 210 young adults after a breakup, those who reflected on it repeatedly regained a clearer sense of who they were. That clearer sense of self predicted less loneliness and fewer intrusive thoughts.

Larson and Sbarra, Social Psychological and Personality Science, 2015

Among 464 people, those who kept checking an ex's profile reported more distress, more longing and less personal growth. The study can't prove checking causes the pain.

Marshall, Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking, 2012

Focusing on an ex's flaws lowered love feelings but made people feel worse in the moment. Distraction lifted mood but didn't change love feelings.

Langeslag and Sanchez, Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 2018
